title: Steady
blurb: PCOS/PMOS is a condition that affects 1 in 10 women, and to this day there is no definitive 'cure' for the immense number of symptoms and issues it brings to those affected. Steady aims to aid women in symptom management as they navigate changes in their bodies, medications, and lifestyle choices.
description:
Living with PCOS/PMOS often means managing a long list of symptoms with very little clarity. Treatments can take months to show results, symptoms shift from week to week, and it is hard to tell whether a new medication or habit is actually making a difference. Many women end up piecing together notes, apps, and memory just to explain how they've been feeling at their next appointment.

Steady is designed to be a calm, steady companion through that process. Rather than promising a cure, it focuses on helping women understand their own bodies: logging symptoms as they happen, keeping track of treatments, and turning that history into patterns they can actually see. The goal is to make the experience feel less overwhelming and to give users something concrete to bring into conversations with their doctors.

Above all, Steady is built around the idea that symptom management is personal. No two experiences with PCOS/PMOS look the same, so the app is meant to adapt to each user rather than fit them into a single template.

devLog.title: A Little Note
devLog.text: Steady is still a developing project, and I am currently working on building some exciting new features, alongside tuning up the existing functionality!

devLog.title: Project kickoff
devLog.text: I started working on the project overview and requirements in June 2026. This phase included research on PCOS/PMOS symptoms and building an in-depth understanding of health tech applications. Most of the resources I used were NIH papers covering both topics.

devLog.title: Prototyping
devLog.text: After laying out all of the required pages (at least initial versions), I began prototyping in Figma, starting with a greyscale version of the pages. Once the landing pages for each feature were built, I added in the desired color palette. This prototype went up for review as part of the Hack Your Summer program and showed the overall flow of the application.

devLog.title: Prototyping continued
devLog.text: Once the initial prototyped pages had gotten some feedback, I began to add in the subpages and add 'functionality' to the buttons and screens in order to show the more advanced flows. This included setting up the sign-up and login flows, along with the visual symptom tracking flows.

devLog.title: Minimum Viable Product (MVP)

Once the landing pages for each feature were built, I added in the desired color palette. This prototype went up for review as part of the Hack Your Summer program and showed the overall flow of the application.

title: FRAMED
tagline: document your favorite media with friends
blurb: Framed was built to connect cinephiles and movie enthusiasts while also providing a platform for sharing reviews and recommendations. The product was built over a 10-week sprint that has since ended, but hopefully development will continue in the future! The highlights of the design are its fun graphics and engaging user experience.
description:
Watching a great movie or show is only half the fun. The other half is talking about it, comparing opinions, and finding out what your friends think you should watch next. Most tracking apps treat logging media as a solo activity, and the social side ends up feeling like an afterthought.

Framed puts friends at the center. Users can log what they watch, rank it against everything else they've seen, and share reviews and recommendations with the people whose taste they trust most. Over time, your profile becomes a record of your taste, and your friends' lists become the best place to find something new.

Just as important as what Framed does is how it feels. Bright colors, playful graphics, and an interface built for exploring make it feel less like a database and more like a space you actually want to spend time in.

devLog.title: Ideation
devLog.text:
Framed is a social media platform that combines what I believe are the best features of some of my favorite apps.

Inspired by the stylistic choices of Superfan, the algorithmic approach of Beli, and the community of Letterboxd, I wanted to build something that I would want to use myself. I've spent a lot of time using these three applications and over time have identified the best and worst features of each in order to make an app that I find optimal.

devLog.title: Feature Selection
devLog.text:
As Product Owner, it was really important for me to carefully select the features of the app that would provide the most value, creating a base product that we could build more detailed features onto.

After discussion and time spent researching other applications, we landed on the basic screens, including our log-in, list page, profile, add content, and friends. As for features, we decided to delay the tastemakers feature, as the ranking algorithm was the most immediate feature a user would want out of the application.

devLog.title: Early Prototypes and Design
devLog.text:
The design of the app was focused on making a fun interface for users, carefully selecting the color palette and buttons in order to emphasize creativity and engagement. The prototype was then built in Figma, showing the basic flows from screen to screen, and we spent 2 weeks working through the design and prototype, gaining user feedback on ease of use and overall experience.

From here, we made adjustments to button placements and other UI elements to improve the overall user experience.

devLog.title: Tech Stack
devLog.text: Given our 10-week time constraint and the need to produce an MVP for competitive purposes, we chose a simple stack. **Firebase** was used for user authentication, **MongoDB** for media storage, **React** for the front end, and the **Simkl API** as our source for TV show and movie information (Letterboxd unfortunately has a notably long waitlist).

title: Laundry Link
tagline: a smart detergent                   dispenser for shared laundry rooms
blurb: Laundry Link is a smart access dispenser for shared laundry rooms, built for the Smart Product Design class. By handing out one pre-measured detergent packet per load, it cuts down on waste and overuse. The final product was pitched to investors and received positive feedback during the Q&A.
description:
Shared laundry rooms come with a familiar set of problems: forgotten detergent, spills, and no easy way to share supplies fairly. Laundry Link replaces the communal bottle with a dispenser that hands out one pre-measured packet at a time to students for free.

Sustainability is at the core of the design. Portioning detergent by load size (full or half) means people use only what they need, which reduces wasted product, excess chemicals going down the drain, and spills. 

The flow is simple. A user enters their finals 4-digits of their ID, the LCD confirms whether the ID is valid and shows their balance, and red and green LEDs give instant feedback. From there, the user picks a full or half load with the two selection buttons, and the matching packet drops into the tray at the front, ready to go into the machine.

Inside, the enclosure is split into three levels: a battery pack, an Arduino Uno with its breadboard, and a servo-driven flip mechanism that dispenses from one of two packet stacks.

Laundry Link was built for the Smart Product Design class. The final product was pitched to a panel of investors, who questioned the team on the concept and design and gave positive feedback.

devLog.title: User Flow
devLog.text: Before building anything, I storyboarded the full interaction in six steps: read the instructions, tap a phone or access card, check your balance, make a load selection, retrieve the packet, and place it into the machine tray.

devLog.title: Enclosure
devLog.text: The exterior houses an instruction panel, an LCD display for ID validation and balance, red and green LED indicators, a keypad for user ID input, and two load selection buttons (full and half). Packets drop into a tray at the front, and the top is removable for refills.

devLog.title: Electronics and Dispensing
devLog.text: The interior is organized into three levels: **battery pack**, **Arduino Uno + breadboard**, and the **dispensing mechanism**. A servo motor drives a flip mechanism that releases a packet from either the full or half load stack, and a master power switch is wired to the battery pack.

devLog.title: Investor Pitch
devLog.text: As the final milestone for Smart Product Design, we pitched Laundry Link to investors and took their questions on the product, its sustainability benefits, and how it would work in a real laundry room. The pitch received positive feedback.
